promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Group behaviour (conformity, social identity, social learning, acculturation, cultural dimensions)
Interpersonal relationships (attraction, chemical messengers, communication, conflict and aggression)

questions.q: Asch's line-judgement studies are best known for demonstrating:
options: Conformity to a majority, even when it is clearly wrong
questions.explain: Participants often agreed with an obviously wrong majority, showing normative social influence.

questions.q: Social identity theory (Tajfel & Turner) explains in-group favouritism through:
options: Social categorisation and the pursuit of positive distinctiveness
questions.explain: Categorising into groups and seeking a positive in-group identity drives favouritism, even in minimal groups.

questions.q: Tajfel's minimal group studies suggest that in-group favouritism can arise from:
options: Mere assignment to a group, even a trivial one
questions.explain: Even meaningless group membership produced favouritism, supporting social categorisation.

questions.q: Bandura's Bobo doll studies demonstrate:
questions.explain: Children imitated an aggressive model, showing behaviour can be learned by observation.

questions.q: Hofstede's 'individualism-collectivism' is:
options: A cultural dimension used to compare cultures
questions.explain: It contrasts emphasis on the individual with emphasis on the group and predicts behaviour such as conformity.

questions.q: Acculturation refers to:
options: Cultural and psychological change from contact with a different culture
questions.explain: Acculturation describes change when individuals or groups have sustained contact with another culture.

questions.q: A person conforms to a group's clearly incorrect answer to avoid standing out. This is best explained by:
questions.explain: Conforming to be accepted or avoid disapproval is normative social influence, as in Asch's studies.

questions.q: 'Vicarious reinforcement' in social learning means a person is more likely to imitate a model who is:
questions.explain: Seeing a model rewarded increases imitation; seeing punishment reduces it.

questions.q: Which pairing is correct?
questions.explain: Tajfel and Turner developed social identity theory; Bandura studied social learning; Asch studied conformity.

questions.q: Factors that increase interpersonal attraction include proximity, similarity and:
questions.explain: Research links attraction to proximity, similarity and physical attractiveness, among other factors.

questions.q: Oxytocin, a chemical messenger linked to bonding, should be interpreted cautiously because:
options: Its effects are context-dependent and replication is mixed
It has no effect on behaviour
questions.explain: Single oxytocin studies (e.g. trust) show context dependence and variable replication.

questions.q: Sherif's Robbers Cave study supports realistic conflict theory by showing that hostility arose from:
options: Competition between groups for scarce resources
A lack of any group identity
questions.explain: Introducing competitive tasks between groups generated prejudice and conflict.

questions.q: In the Robbers Cave study, conflict was most effectively reduced by:
questions.explain: Shared goals neither group could achieve alone required cooperation and reduced hostility.

questions.q: A cognitive explanation of relationship satisfaction focuses on:
options: How partners appraise and make attributions about each other
questions.explain: Cognitive accounts stress appraisals and attributions in shaping satisfaction.

questions.q: Aggression is best explained as:
options: Multiply determined — biological, cognitive and social factors together
questions.explain: Aggression has biological correlates (e.g. testosterone) and social-learning roots, plus cognitive factors.

questions.q: Two teams become hostile while competing for a limited prize, then cooperate when given a shared goal. This illustrates:
options: Realistic conflict theory and superordinate goals
questions.explain: Competition for scarce resources drives conflict; superordinate goals reduce it.

questions.q: Which is a 'chemical messenger' relevant to relationships?
questions.explain: Oxytocin is a hormone/neuropeptide associated with bonding and trust.

questions.q: A limitation of many laboratory studies of group behaviour is that they:
options: May lack ecological validity despite good control
questions.explain: Tight control aids internal validity, but artificial settings may not reflect real-world behaviour.

questions.q: Classic social-influence studies (Asch, Milgram) raised ethical concerns mainly about:
options: Deception and psychological stress, requiring debriefing
questions.explain: These studies involved deception and potential distress, so thorough debriefing was essential.

questions.q: A researcher wants strong evidence that a factor CAUSES aggression. The most appropriate design is:
options: A controlled experiment with a comparison group
questions.explain: Only a controlled experiment can support a causal claim about aggression.
